tagline.text: Highland vegetables, strawberries and souvenirs: Baguio's kitchen

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,500 (including souvenirs and food, per person)

children.text: Baguio City Market is Baguio's best-known traditional market, running along Magsaysay Avenue. It brings together highland vegetables and strawberries that arrive daily from La Trinidad, plus souvenirs such as peanut brittle and ube jam. The shops open from early in the morning, and it is liveliest if you go before noon.

Baguio City Market is a traditional market spread widely along Magsaysay Avenue in downtown Baguio. The address is sometimes given as 38 Rajah Soliman Street, but the actual shops spread across the area where the lower end of Session Road meets Magsaysay Avenue. Malcolm Square lies across from it, and if you walk over from Session Road you enter the market by crossing the pedestrian overpass at the square.

Here you can buy highland vegetables such as carrots, potatoes, broccoli, cauliflower and lettuce, brought in every day from La Trinidad, for less than in Manila. From November to April strawberries are in season, and many souvenirs are sold, such as strawberry jam, ube jam and peanut brittle. Indigenous handicraft shops, secondhand clothing shops (ukay-ukay), meat and seafood sections and a cut-flower section are all gathered in one place. Besides carrots and broccoli, you also find lemons, sayote tops and herbs such as parsley, and one guide says the vegetables are cheaper than in Manila.

The market is not a single building but a series of connected sections. On the Magsaysay Avenue side is the Maharlika Livelihood Complex, with its eye-catching Cordillera-style roof, and if you go up toward Hilltop Street and Kayang Street at the back of the market you come to meat stalls, market arcades and secondhand clothing shops. The jeepney terminals are close by, so the market also serves as a gateway to the surroundings of Baguio.

The market is packed with small shops and stalls, and time flies as you walk. One guide suggests allowing 1–2 hours for a visit. Prices differ by shop and by season, so there is some fun in bargaining and comparing as you buy. Reviews say the market is relatively clean and the vendors friendly, and some reviews wish there were a separate area for loading and pickup of vehicles.
Carrots, potatoes, broccoli, cauliflower and lettuce arrive daily from La Trinidad. The cheapest place is said to be the Hangar section, deeper inside past the rice and coffee sections.

Strawberries are in season roughly from November to April and are sold near the handicrafts and T-shirt section. Bigger berries cost more. Choose less ripe ones and keep them dry, and they travel home well.

Peanut brittle, made of finely chopped peanuts spread thin, is the market's signature souvenir. You can also find lengua de gato, alfajor, chocolate-coated corn flakes and sundot kulangot. Peanut brittle is sold in small and large jars, and the price depends on the size and the quality of the peanuts.
Ube jam is a spread you can put on bread or eat by the spoon like ube halaya. The Good Shepherd brand is famous, and the market also has many cheaper brands.
Coffee stalls in the market sell Arabica beans from Benguet, Kalinga and Sagada, as whole beans or ground.
You can find baskets, wooden plates, woodcrafts and handwoven wallets and keychains. If you buy in quantity you can get a discount. This section comes before the strawberry and souvenir section.

If you go from Kayang Street past the meat market and up Hilltop Street, there are many secondhand clothing shops. In 2018 the reported prices were blouses and shirts from ₱30, jackets at ₱60 and jeans under ₱150.
Fresh flowers such as roses and mums are sold cheaply. Ready-made arrangements are near Abanao Square, and loose flowers are in the Hangar section, nearly opposite Baguio Center Mall.

items.title: Morning route of 1–2 hours
items.subtitle: Vegetables, strawberries and souvenirs in that order

children.text: Enter the market by the overpass from the Session Road side. The meat and vegetable shops that have been open since dawn are liveliest at this hour.
Walk through the vegetable section and the Hangar and look at fresh vegetables and herbs. Basil, rosemary, mint and parsley are also sold.
Move on to the strawberry and souvenir sections. Compare prices on strawberries, jam, ube jam and peanut brittle before you buy.
Look at baskets and wooden plates in the handicraft section.
Buy longganisa on Kayang Street behind the market and, if you like, browse the secondhand clothing shops on the Hilltop side.
Weekends are crowded, so the earlier you arrive, the faster you can get around.

items.title: From downtown Baguio to the market

children.text: You can walk from Session Road. Cross the overpass at Malcolm Square and you are at the Magsaysay Avenue side of the market.
By taxi it is a short ride from anywhere downtown. Traffic around the market is congested and parking can be difficult, so it is better to go on foot.
Near the market there are jeepney terminals on Kayang Street and Otek Street, where you can board jeepneys toward the BenCab Museum and Tam-awan Village.
The market spans several streets and it is easy to get lost at first. Use the Maharlika Livelihood Complex and Malcolm Square as reference points.

The market is open all year, but November to April is best if you want strawberries. During this season many strawberries arrive from La Trinidad. During the Panagbenga Flower Festival in February downtown is crowded, so the market may be crowded as well.

There are many snack stalls in the market. In the early morning vendors walk around selling "strawberry taho" with strawberry syrup, which costs slightly more than regular taho. Restaurants, cafés and lodging cluster around nearby Session Road and Burnham Park, so it is easy to rest after you finish at the market.
Lodging is plentiful in the downtown area between the market and Session Road. Staying near the market makes it easy to shop at dawn. Check prices and location before you book.

It helps to list the best gifts from the market. For strawberry jam and ube jam, Good Shepherd is the leading brand, and the Good Shepherd store at the Mountain Maid Training Center sells a wider range. Raisin bread originated at the Baguio Country Club, and you can buy it by entering as a member's guest or at the mall stalls where the club sells it. For silver jewelry it is better to look at the shops on Session Road, and at the market brooms (walis) are popular with locals. Chocolate corn flakes come in small and large jars, and sundot kulangot is packed in half coconut shells tied with a red paper band.

Food is part of the market visit. In the early morning strawberry taho vendors walk around, and at lunchtime you can use the restaurants around the market and the shops on Session Road. Check menus and prices at each place.
Pick less ripe strawberries and keep them dry. It also helps to ask the vendor to pack them so they do not bruise. In season they stay fresh for about 3 days, according to a vendor.
Many visitors say the Hangar section has the cheapest vegetables. Go past the rice and coffee sections and head inside.
Reviews say peanut brittle and jam are cheaper at the market than at shops near the bus terminals. Compare before you buy.
Bargaining is possible, and vendors sometimes add a free item when you buy several.
Beware of pickpockets in the evening crowds. Wear your bag in front and keep valuables separate.
The handicraft section and the souvenir section are close to each other, and the handicraft section comes before the strawberry and souvenir section. Decide your route through the market in advance.
If you go early in the morning you can also meet the strawberry taho vendors.
Small shops may be short of change, so carry small bills.
Peanut brittle and jam come in large and small jars, so compare sizes if you are buying gifts.
There are reports of pickpockets at the market during crowded hours. Wear your bag in front and do not show valuables.
On crowded weekends and during festivals it is hard to move around and prices may rise.
Parking around the market is difficult. Walking or a taxi is better than driving.
The floors in the meat and fish sections are wet, so wear shoes that will not slip.
In the crowded evening hours stalls are set up quickly and it gets congested, so finish your shopping in the morning if you can.

Redevelopment of the market is still under discussion. SM Prime's 2025 public-private proposal was reported withdrawn in January 2026 and the city is said to be reconsidering its approach, so the layout of the sections may change in the future.
